Non- 250 interventional studies also include those involving primary data collection (e.g. prospective 251 observational studies and registries in which the data collected derive from routine clinical care), 252 provided that the conditions set out above are met. 253 In this context, interviews, questionnaires and blood samples may be peformed as normal clinical 254 practice. 255 Occupational exposure 256 An exposure to a medicinal product for human use as a result of one’s occupation. 257 Ongoing clinical trial 258 Trial where enrolment has begun, whether a hold is in place or analysis is complete, but for which a 259 final clinical study report is not available (see ICH-E2F Guideline, Volume 10 of the Rules Governing 260 Medicinal Products in the EU). 261 See also

candidates.statement: EMA/876333/2011 Page 12/14 To this end, it must identify or characterise the safety profile of the medicinal product(s) concerned; 352 indicate how to characterise further the safety profile of the medicinal product(s) concerned; document 353 measures to prevent minimise the risks associated with the medicinal product, including an 354 assessment of the effectiveness of those interventions; and document post-authorisation obligations 355 that have been imposed as a condition of the marketing authorisation [IM Annex II.1.]. 356 See also Risk management system, Risk minimisation activity 357 Risk management system 358 A set of pharmacovigilance activities and interventions designed to identify, characterise, prevent or 359 minimise risks relating to a medicinal product, including the assessment of the effectiveness of those 360 interventions [DIR 2001/83/EC Art 1(28b)]. 361 Risk minimisation activity; synonym: Risk minimisation measure 362 A public health intervention intended to prevent or reduce the probability of the occurrence of an 363 adverse reaction associated with the exposure to a medicine, or to reduce its severity should it occur 364 (see Annex IV, ICH-E2C(R2) Guideline). 365 These activities may consist of routine risk minimisation (e.g. product information) or additional risk 366 minimisation activities (e.g. healthcare professional or patient communications/educational materials) 367 (see Annex IV, ICH-E2C(R2) Guideline). 368 Risks related to use of a medicinal product 369 Any risk relating to the quality, safety or efficacy of the medicinal product as regards patients’ health 370

candidates.statement: or public health and any risk of undesirable effects on the environment [DIR 2001/83/EC Art 1(28)]. 371 Safety concern 372 An important identified risk, important potential risk or important missing information (see Annex IV, 373 ICH-E2C(R2) Guideline). 374 See also Important identified risk and Important potential risk, Important missing information 375 Serious adverse reaction 376 Serious adverse reaction means an adverse reaction which results in death, is life-threatening, requires 377 in-patient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation, results in persistent or significant 378 disability or incapacity, or is a congenital anomaly/birth defect [DIR 2001/83/EC Art 1(12)]. 379 Life-threatening in this context refers to a reaction in which the patient was at risk of death at the time 380 of the reaction; it does not refer to a reaction that hypothetically might have caused death if more 381 severe (see Annex IV, ICH-E2D Guideline). 382 Medical and scientific judgement should be exercised in deciding whether other situations should be 383 considered serious reactions, such as important medical events that might not be immediately life 384 threatening or result in death or hospitalisation but might jeopardise the patient or might require 385 intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed above. Examples of such events are intensive 386 treatment in an emergency room or at home for allergic bronchospasm, blood dyscrasias or 387 convulsions that do not result in hospitalisation or development of dependency or abuse (see Annex IV, 388 ICH-E2D Guideline). 389

candidates.statement: EMA/876333/2011 Page 13/14 Any suspected transmission via a medicinal product of an infectious agent is also considered a serious 390 adverse reaction. 391 See also Adverse reaction 392 Signal 393 Information arising from one or multiple sources, including observations and experiments, which 394 suggests a new potentially causal association, or a new aspect of a known association, between an 395 intervention and an event or set of related events, either adverse or beneficial, that is judged to be of 396 sufficient likelihood to justify verificatory action [IM Art 23(1)]. 397 For the purpose of the EudraVigilance database, only signals related to an adverse reaction shall be 398 considered [IM Art 23(2)111]. 399 See also Validated signal, Newly identified signal, Closed signal, Ongoing signal 400 Significant change in indication 401 A significant change in indication is a change of authorised indication(s) of a medicinal product where 402 the new treatment target population differs materially from the one for which the medicinal product 403 was previously authorised. This includes (but is not limited to): a new disease area, a new age group 404 (e.g. paediatric indication) or a move from severe disease to a less severely affected population. It 405 may also include a move from second line or other therapy or for an oncology product a change to the 406 concomitant medication specified in the indication. 407 See also Target population (treatment) 408 Solicited sources of individual case safety reports 409 Organised data collection systems, which include clinical trials, registries, post-authorisation named- 410

candidates.statement: patients use programmes, other patient support and disease management programmes, surveys of 411 patients or healthcare providers or information gathering on efficacy or patient compliance. 412 For the purpose of safety reporting, solicited reports should be classified as individual case safety 413 reports from studies and therefore should have an appropriate causality assessment by a healthcare 414 professional or the marketing authorisation holder (see Annex IV, ICH-E2D). 415 See also Clinical trial, Post-authorisation safety study, Non-interventional study 416 Spontaneous report, synonym: Spontaneous notification 417 An unsolicited communication by a healthcare professional or consumer to a company, regulatory 418 authority or other organisation (e.g. the World Health Organization, a regional centre, a poison control 419 centre) that describes one or more adverse reactions in a patient who was given one or more 420 medicinal products and that does not derive from a study or any organised data collection scheme (see 421 Annex IV, ICH-E2D). 422 In this context, an adverse reaction refers to a suspected adverse reaction. 423 Stimulated reporting can occur in certain situations, such as direct healthcare professional 424 communication (DHPC), a publication in the press or questioning of healthcare professionals by 425 company representatives, and adverse reaction reports arising from these situations are considered 426 spontaneous reports (see Annex IV, ICH-E2D), provided the report meets the definition above. 427
